title: an Action input projecting a field the durable descriptor does not have is refused, and the diagnostic names that Action's input

diagnostics.messageContains: #Step input cannot project length from durable array

notes: specification/durable-execution.mdx:49 (Durable Boundary Contract): 'Every value crossing an Action or Flow persistence boundary MUST satisfy the compiler-checked durable codec contract.' Read with :63, 'Property access and argument passing on a symbolic result MUST create typed projections and dependency edges when representable in Plan IR', and :71, 'Runtime-dependent control flow MUST be represented explicitly in Plan IR. The compiler MUST reject an operation that would inspect a symbolic value without a corresponding IR representation.' An Action's input is a value crossing the boundary exactly as the Flow's output is, so a path the durable descriptor cannot answer is refused there too. WHAT THIS CASE IS FOR: until 2026-08-27 BOTH implementations compiled this program and ran it, and the Plan they emitted carried {"kind":"input","path":["items","length"]} into the executor's `pathValue`, which faults on a non-numeric part of an array with a ProjectionDefect -- a compile-time-knowable error deferred into a runtime defect on both backends at once. It survived the two earlier repairs because the Flow's OUTPUT here is a bare node reference the descriptor answers perfectly, so an output-only walk cannot see the defect one level in. `.length` is the sharp spelling: TypeScript accepts it on an array, so no assignability rule fires first and the refusal has to come from the durable descriptor. THE DECLARED POSITION: 11:29 is the `(` of the arrow function, not the projection. Both implementations anchor this rule on the durable source function because the descriptor that could not answer the path is the Flow's boundary contract rather than any one expression -- the same anchor the other SMITHERS4110 boundary refusals use. WHY messageContains: the repair works by having every failure site drop a hard-coded "Flow output " prefix and letting the collecting walk prepend the subject of the value it is visiting, so the SUBJECT is precisely what changed and precisely what a code-and-position expectation cannot see; an implementation that refused this program while still calling it the Flow output would satisfy the first three fields exactly. The fragment is the smallest one that carries the promise -- the subject and the projected field and the kind it was projected from -- and deliberately stops short of the whole sentence and of the `.sm` file name in front of `#Step`, because message wording is not the contract and a fragment naming this file would be about the case rather than about the rule. VERIFIED LOAD-BEARING, not assumed: five mutations were run through both backends, each one red on BOTH with the diff printed -- line 11 to 12, column 29 to 30, SMITHERS4110 to SMITHERS4111, `durable array` to `durable string` in the fragment, and `#Step input cannot project` to `Flow output cannot project` in the fragment (that last one is the regression the subject pins). The mutator refuses to run unless the case is green on both backends first AND its search string occurs exactly once in the file, and the file was restored and sha256-compared byte-identical after every one. The paired positive control is an-action-input-projection-the-descriptor-can-answer-is-accepted, which is this program with the projection swapped and nothing else touched. NO MARKER on either backend: one diagnostic each, same code, line, column and sentence, so `Markers holding a fail-open` stays 0. PROGRAMS THIS CASE DELIBERATELY IS NOT: a spelling carrying `!` (the reference draws a second diagnostic, SMITHERS1207, that the fork does not, and the judge compares full diagnostic lists), `input.obj.missing` (JS reports SMITHERS4100 via TS2339, Go reports SMITHERS4110), and `input.pair[5]` / `.toFixed` / `.valueOf` (same code on both, different sentence and column). Every one of those would need an xfail for a pre-existing reason unrelated to this rule.
